newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian mum defends son in extortion affair.
newsitem.headline: Australian mum defends son in extortion affair.

text.p: The mother of a man being sought over Australia's poison-cookies blackmail bid said her son loved children and would never do anything that could hurt them, media reports said Saturday.

"He's got children of his own, nieces and nephews. They love biscuits (cookies), why try to do them harm?" Irene Oliphant said of her son, John Bobak, whom police want to question over an extortion bid that has hit one of the country's most prominent companies, Arnotts Ltd.

Arnotts, Australia's largest cookie-maker, Friday ordered its products off the shelves of shops along the heavily-populated east coast after a blackmailer threatened to plant poisoned cookies in shops starting Monday.
Authorities have received samples of poisoned cookies and have warned that just one could kill a child.

The extortionist has demanded that police involved in a 1991 murder case take a lie detector test in an attempt to prove the innocence of a man jailed for life for the execution-style murder of a bookmaker and his girlfriend.
There is a long-standing warrant for Bobak over the 1991 killings, but police would not say officially if he was a suspect in the extortion.

The extortionist laced Monte Carlo cream cookies made by Arnotts with a pesticide and sent six packets of the poisoned cookies, along with a letter, to Arnotts, politicians and a media organisation in the states of New South Wales and Queensland on Feb. 3, police said.
The letter demanded that New South Wales police involved in the murder investigation of bookmaker Peter Wade and his girlfriend in 1991 take a lie detector test by Monday.
The letter said Ronald Thomas, 46, convicted of the shooting murders, was innocent and that the real killers remained free.
Police have rejected the extortionist's demand.
Arnotts, about 70 percent owned by U.S. food processing giant Campbell Soup Co., of Philadelphia, said Saturday it was continuing to make cookies for sale overseas and in other areas of Australia.

Managing director Chris Roberts told a news conference the company was flying machinery in from overseas to make its packets tamper-proof and could have its products back on the shelves within 10 days.
The extortion threat and a 14 percent drop in half-year profits announced Friday saw millions of dollars wiped off the company's value as shares plunged 3 percent.
